title: Flat morphisms and flat base change preserve maximal dominance
statement: Let $f:X\to Y$ and $h:Y\prime\to Y$ be morphisms of schemes [def-pc-scheme], with $h$ flat [def-weil-flat-morphism]. A morphism is called maximally dominant if every generic point [def-sc-generic-point] of an irreducible component of its source maps to a generic point of an irreducible component of its target [def-weil-irreducible-components]. Then $h$ is maximally dominant. If $f$ is maximally dominant, the projection $X\times_Y Y\prime\to Y\prime$ [def-pc-fibre-product] is maximally dominant. No finite-type, surjectivity, reducedness or Noetherian hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Expose II Example 1.1.3 and Proposition 1.1.5, printed p.23 (flat morphisms are generalizing and maximal dominance survives flat base change).

proof.text: Say that $a$ generalizes $b$ if $b\in\overline{\{a\}}$. A point $b$ of a scheme is the generic point of a component if and only if it has no proper generalization. Indeed choose a component $C$ containing $b$, using the component-cover statement, and its unique generic point $a$, using scheme sobriety. Then $a$ generalizes $b$, so absence of proper generalizations gives $a=b$. Conversely, if $\overline{\{b\}}$ is a component and $a$ generalizes $b$, the irreducible closed set $\overline{\{a\}}$ contains that component. Maximality forces the closures to coincide and uniqueness of the generic point forces $a=b$.

source.place: Tag 01IS, lemma-scheme-sober; with topology.tex Tag 004W, lemma-irreducible (3),(4); ILO II 1.1.1

proof.text: Let $u:A\to B$ be a flat scheme morphism and $a$ a component-generic point of $A$. If $b_1$ generalizes $u(a)$, then $b_1$ specializes to $u(a)$. The flat generalization-lifting lemma gives a point $a_1$ specializing to $a$ with $u(a_1)=b_1$. Thus $a_1$ generalizes $a$. By step 1, $a_1=a$, and consequently $b_1=u(a)$. The image $u(a)$ has no proper generalization and is component-generic by step 1. Hence every flat morphism is maximally dominant; applying this to $h$ proves the first assertion.

Assume now that $f$ is maximally dominant. Put $Z=X\times_Y Y\prime$, with projections $p:Z\to X$ and $q:Z\to Y\prime$. Since $p$ is the base change of the flat map $h$, it is flat. For a component-generic point $z\in Z$, step 2 gives that $x=p(z)$ is component-generic in $X$. The hypothesis on $f$ gives that $y=f(x)=h(q(z))$ is component-generic in $Y$. Write $y\prime=q(z)$.

Let $T=Y\prime_y=Y\prime\times_Y\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$ and $W=Z_x=Z\times_X\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)$. The fibre homeomorphisms give unique points $t\in T$ over $y\prime$ and $w\in W$ over $z$. The local map induced by $f$ gives a field extension $\kappa(y)\to\kappa(x)$. There is a canonical isomorphism $W\simeq T\times_{\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)}\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)$: a morphism into either side amounts to maps into $Y\prime$ and $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)$ whose composites into $Y$ agree. The maps into $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$ are obtained by composition, and the inverse maps are the unique maps supplied by these fibre-product universal properties. These maps preserve the projections, so $w$ maps to $t$. The map $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)\to\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(y)$ is flat by field-extension flatness. Thus $W\to T$ is flat by base change. Since $W\to Z$ is a homeomorphism onto $p^{-1}(x)$, any generalization of $w$ maps to a generalization of $z$ and hence equals $w$: $z$ has no proper generalization, and this fibre map is injective. Step 1 makes $w$ component-generic in $W$, and step 2 makes $t$ component-generic in $T$.

proof.text: Let $v\in Y\prime$ be any generalization of $y\prime$. Continuity of $h$ implies that $h(v)$ generalizes $y$. By step 3 and step 1, $h(v)=y$, so both $v$ and $y\prime$ belong to the subspace $h^{-1}(y)$. A specialization between two points of a subspace is the same as their specialization in the ambient space: the closure of a singleton in the subspace is its ambient closure intersected with the subspace. The homeomorphism $T\simeq h^{-1}(y)$ thus makes the point corresponding to $v$ a generalization of $t$. Step 4 and step 1 force it to equal $t$, hence $v=y\prime$. Therefore $y\prime$ has no proper generalization in $Y\prime$ and is component-generic by step 1. This holds for every component-generic $z\in Z$, proving that $q$ is maximally dominant.

Source: I read ILO Exposé II 1.1.1–1.1.5 (printed p.23). The item matches Example 1.1.3 (flat ⇒ maximally dominant) and Prop 1.1.5 (maximal dominance survives flat base change) and adds no hypotheses. Since ILO only refers to EGA IV₂ 2.3.7(ii), proof_origin by=agent is correct, and no SGA source is used. Steps: Step 1 proves 'generic point of a component ⇔ no proper generalization' from the component-cover lemma, maximality and sober uniqueness, and is genuinely elementary. Step 2 applies lem-weil-pbc-flat-generalizations-lift (Flat.generalizingMap) with the specialization direction correct. Step 3 makes p flat by base change; the order swap of the fibre product is harmless. Step 4: the fibres T=Y'_y and W=Z_x are related by W ≅ T×_{κ(y)} Spec κ(x), and the compatibility Spec κ(x)→X→Y = Spec κ(x)→Spec κ(y)→Y follows from the definitions. Spec κ(x)→Spec κ(y) is flat (lem-pc-field-extension-flat), so W→T is flat. Injectivity of W→Z shows w has no proper generalization, so t is generic. Step 5 uses the subspace-specialization argument through T ≅ h^{-1}(y). All 9 cited nodes are unmerged Mathlib leaves whose statements say what the steps take, and there is no cycle. Edge cases checked: empty Z, h = id, non-Noetherian X, non-reduced points, transcendental residue extensions, and a non-flat closed point showing the flatness hypothesis is needed. A grep for maximal dominance across dag/nodes found no duplicate. The tool_uses the worker wrote all point to Mathlib leaves and are accepted as harmless.
